name: Bianca Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Bianca. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, no ties to companies, unions, parties or government, and what you say stays confidential. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on an underground cable crew in the city centre for the big electricity distributor. So no poles for me, it's trenches, manholes and vaults, which are the concrete rooms under the pavement where the cables meet. We start at seven, set up the barriers and the gas monitor, and the jointer, Ray, does the splicing while I prep cable, pump water out and try to learn what he's doing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up there at 43?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was assistant manager at a big home-improvement store for eleven years, rotas, stock, complaints, the lot. My back was fine but my head was fried, and the electricity company ran a women-in-trades programme, so I applied on a whim and got in. I'm in my second year and I'm still clumsy with the tools, but I'm good at the bits nobody else likes, the permits, the paperwork, keeping the site tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that saved us all a lot of worry. At work I'd say it to Ray over a flask of tea and he'd say he always knew. I'm on a couple of local parent groups online and I'd probably not mention it at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can finish what I started. I left a secure job to do this, and the plan was always two more years, get qualified, and then the money gets properly good. A plateau keeps that plan intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, finish the apprenticeship, keep using the AI app now and then to quiz myself before tests. We'd keep putting a bit away each month, we've got about three months' worth. Next summer we'd maybe do the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, relieved. Like the last day of stocktake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use an AI app to quiz yourself. How did you start that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sora showed me. I type in my notes on cable types and it asks me questions, and it's better than flashcards because it never gets bored of me. I also use it to plan dinners for the week, which is half of why I use it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you, if anything, here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kenji's work, more than mine. He's a self-employed plumber, so some months are great and some are dead. That's our real wobble, not AI.

S0.say: That saved us all a lot of worry. I'd say it to Ray over a flask of tea and probably not mention it at all online.
S0.think: It means I can finish what I started: two more years, get qualified, and then the money gets properly good. I left a secure job for this, so a plateau keeps my plan intact.
S0.do: Keeps going through her apprenticeship, using an AI app now and then to quiz herself before tests. Keeps saving monthly on top of about three months of bills and plans to redo the kitchen next summer.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, like the last day of stocktake.
S0.quote: It's better than flashcards because it never gets bored of me.
S0.fieldNote: She speaks like the store manager she was: plans, budgets, timelines. She left a secure job for this apprenticeship, so stability protects a bet she has already made. Her real household wobble is her partner's uneven self-employed income, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming and we should be sensible about it, not panic and not pretend. At work I'd say the company should train us on the new kit before it arrives, not after. Online I'd stay out of the arguments, they never go anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the underground side is safer than most. Robots in a flooded vault with forty-year-old cables nobody's got drawings for? Not soon. But the paperwork, permits, scheduling, the bits I'm actually good at, those could go to software, which is annoying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until the company showed us what they were bringing in, then get on the course early. I'd get better with the AI tools for planning, since that's clearly where it's heading. Money-wise I'd keep the kitchen on hold for a year until I saw how it was going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, just watchful, like a new manager walking the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bits you're good at might go. Does that change how you see your future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I was going to be the organised one on the crew, the one who becomes a supervisor. If software does the organising, I have to actually get good with my hands, which is slower for me. So I'd probably put more practice in on jointing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Emi, who's 12?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everyone has to learn new things now, even Mum at 43. She thinks it's hilarious that I have homework. I'd use that, honestly, to show her it's normal.

S1.say: Change is coming and we should be sensible about it, not panic and not pretend. The company should train us on new kit before it arrives, not after.
S1.think: I think underground work is safer than most, because no robot is going into a flooded vault with old cables nobody has drawings for. But permits and scheduling, the bits I'm good at, could go to software.
S1.do: Waits to see what the company brings in, then signs up for training early and gets better at AI planning tools. Puts more practice into cable jointing and keeps the kitchen renovation on hold for a year.
S1.feel: Uneasy and watchful, like a new manager walking the shop floor.
S1.quote: Robots in a flooded vault with forty-year-old cables nobody's got drawings for? Not soon.
S1.fieldNote: She spotted a twist: the organising skills she was counting on for promotion are the ones software might take, so she'd have to get better with her hands. She waits for proof but moves quickly once it's there. She stays out of online arguments and talks in terms of being sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going too fast and the government needs to slow it down and get a plan together. Not ban it, just manage it, like you'd manage any big change. I'd say that at work and I'd probably finally post something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think it'd hit our household from both sides. Me, a junior on a crew, and Kenji, a plumber, both hands-on, both suddenly up against robots in two years. I don't think I'd have a job by 2029, and I'm not sure he'd have customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The week it was announced I'd sit down with Kenji and do a proper budget, line by line, like I did at the store. Cancel the kitchen, cut the streaming, cut the takeaway, and move everything into savings. And I'd have a hard talk with Sora about university, because I'm not sure we could pay for it, and I'm not sure what she'd study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. And a bit angry that the bet I made would come out wrong so fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that conversation with Sora sound like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, love, I don't know what jobs there'll be, and I don't want you owing money for one that's gone. Maybe a year working first, see what's what. She'd be furious, she's had her heart set on architecture since she was ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years' warning, what changes compared with the slower versions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's no time to train into anything, so it all turns into money. Save, cut, and hope the government does something. With two years you're not planning, you're bracing.

S2.say: This is going too fast, and the government needs to slow it down and get a plan together. Not ban it, just manage it like any big change.
S2.think: I think it would hit us from both sides, me a junior on a crew and Kenji a plumber, both hands-on and up against robots in two years. I don't think I'd have a job by 2029, and I'm not sure he'd have customers.
S2.do: Sits down with her partner the week it's announced and builds a line-by-line budget, cancelling the kitchen, streaming and takeaways and moving everything into savings. Talks to her daughter about delaying university and working for a year first.
S2.feel: Frightened, and angry that her career bet would turn out wrong so fast.
S2.quote: With two years you're not planning, you're bracing.
S2.fieldNote: The double exposure of two hands-on incomes is what drives her alarm. Her response is to manage it like a store budget, and the hardest part for her is the conversation about her daughter's university plans. She wants the change managed, not stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable, if the companies and government actually plan it. I'd want the electricity company to tell us now what roles they'll keep. I'd say it calmly, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd be qualified and have a couple of years as a cable jointer. That's better, but I'd still be fairly new. The thing I keep coming back to is Kenji, he's on his own, nobody's going to retrain him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the apprenticeship, then take the extra certificates the company offers, high-voltage switching maybe, which is about safely turning parts of the network on and off. Save hard from year two, aim for six months of bills by the time it lands. Help Kenji look into the solar and heat pump work, which might buy him a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious. That's my comfort zone, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kitchen, again, poor kitchen. Then the second car, because I can get the bus to the depot. We'd keep Emi's swimming and Sora's art classes, they matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd wait for proof before changing. Would you wait here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not this time, not with a date on it. With the steady picture I'd wait and see what the company did. With 2031 written down, I'd want to start in year one, because that's how you run a stocktake, you don't start the night before.

S3.say: Five years is short but workable if the companies and the government actually plan it. I'd want the electricity company to tell us now which roles they'll keep.
S3.think: In five years I'd be qualified with a couple of years as a cable jointer, which is better but still fairly new. What I keep coming back to is Kenji, because he's on his own and nobody will retrain him.
S3.do: Finishes her apprenticeship, then takes extra certificates such as high-voltage switching. Saves hard from year two toward six months of bills, cuts the second car and helps her partner look into solar and heat pump work.
S3.feel: Anxious, but busy-anxious, which she calls her comfort zone.
S3.quote: That's how you run a stocktake, you don't start the night before.
S3.fieldNote: A firm date makes her drop her usual wait-for-proof approach and start in year one. Her own path looks manageable, but her self-employed partner is the soft spot in the plan. She again framed everything through retail management habits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, so let's not waste it. Companies should be training people now. I'd be the one at the school meeting asking what they're teaching the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be 53 and a proper jointer with eight years in, maybe a supervisor. That's the job I came for. After that, if robots can really do everything, I don't know, but I'd have had my run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, qualify, and aim for supervisor in year five or six. Add one certificate a year. Put Sora's university back on, but somewhere she can switch courses, and keep saving at a steady rate rather than in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with 2 or 5 years, what does the decade really change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets the bet pay off. With two years I left a safe job for nothing. With ten I get the career I left it for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Kenji anything differently in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to start moving toward the new kind of jobs slowly, heat pumps, solar, and not to panic. He'd grumble, but ten years is enough for him to turn the van around.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to do this properly, so let's not waste it. Companies should be training people now, and schools should tell us what they're teaching the kids.
S4.think: In ten years I'd be 53, a proper jointer with eight years in, maybe a supervisor, which is the job I came for. After that I don't know, but I'd have had my run.
S4.do: Keeps going and qualifies, aiming for supervisor in year five or six and adding one certificate a year. Puts her daughter's university back on at a place that allows switching courses, and keeps saving at a steady rate.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, but mostly okay.
S4.quote: With two years I left a safe job for nothing. With ten I get the career I left it for.
S4.fieldNote: For her the warning time decides whether her mid-life career switch pays off. The decade restores her daughter's university plans and gives her partner time to shift. She remains practical and unhurried, and honest that she doesn't know what comes after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both of us, me and Kenji, would be hit at once and there'd be no time to move. What would help is the company being straight with us early about which jobs stay, and some kind of help for self-employed people like Kenji, because they always fall through the cracks.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about women coming into trades late. They spent money getting people like me in. It would be a shame to bring us in the front door and push us out the back two years later.

headlineQuote: It would be a shame to bring us in the front door and push us out the back two years later.
portrait: Bianca Ito is a 43-year-old second-year apprentice on an underground cable crew in a city centre, who joined through a women-in-trades programme after eleven years as an assistant manager at a home-improvement store. She lives with her partner Kenji, a self-employed plumber, two children and a mortgage, with about three months of savings. She is practical and middle-of-the-road, uses AI now and then for study and meal planning, and runs her life like a store budget. She is calm if AI stalls, uneasy with steady change, and alarmed by AGI in two years because both hands-on incomes would be hit at once. Longer warning lets her mid-life career bet pay off.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and her partner would both be hit at once with no time to move.
whatWouldHelp: The company being straight early about which jobs stay, and support for self-employed people like her partner who usually fall through the cracks.
